D:\\wt\\ssimple2\\vlog\\ssimple2\\voz\\b.text: This is my mother at 95, in her little kitchen in Osaka, and she lived 6 more years after this picture. She died at 101, in the same small wooden house where she raised 5 children. After she turned 60, she did not start a lot of new things. She stopped doing 9 things. Today I will tell you all 9, the way she told them to me. And number nine is sitting in your cupboard right now, wrapped in paper, waiting for a day that is never coming. One of them she did every single morning at 6.30 in the park with 40 neighbors. Another one is a little notebook she kept by her pillow for almost 40 years. But first, one honest thing. I cannot promise you a hundred and one. Nobody can. This is not advice from a clinic. This is just how one old woman lived, busy and happy, until the very last year.

I am 79 now, and I do every one of these nine things. You know me. I'm Sachiko. I was born in Osaka in 1948, the fourth of five children, and I came to America in 1970 with my husband. My mother was born in 1915. She lived through the war and the hungry years after it, and she outlived almost everybody she knew. Come, sit with me, and I will tell you about her. When my father died, my mother was 61. My brothers and sisters and I thought she would get small and quiet, the way some widows do. We talked on the telephone about who would take her in. Then I got a letter from her, three pages, in her beautiful handwriting. It said, Do not worry about me. I have decided to stop doing some things, and she did. She stopped them one by one, over the next few years, like taking stones out of her pockets.

She lived 40 more years in that house. Every summer when I visited, she was a little lighter. Number one, she stopped rushing. My mother said, It means, if you are in a hurry, take the long way around. When you rush, you drop the eggs, you miss the step, you say the wrong thing. So she left the house 15 minutes early for everything. The market, the post office, the temple, the bus. She never ran for a bus in 40 years. She said, the next bus is also a bus. When I was young, I thought she was just slow. Now I understand. She was never late and she never fell. She did the same with her words. When somebody asked her a hard question, she counted to three in her head before she answered. One, two, three. In those three seconds, she said, most foolish answers walk away by themselves. I do the same here.

If my appointment is at 10, I leave at 9.15. If I am early, I sit in the car and I listen to the radio or I look at the trees. Nobody ever got hurt sitting in a car looking at a tree. Rushing is what old people do when they forget they are old. Before I tell you number two, if you are new here, this little channel is about living simple after 60, the way my mother did. Please press subscribe so the next video finds you. And if you like to cook, come see my kitchen channel too, where I show you her Osaka kitchen tricks. Number 2. She stopped buying things on the first day. When my mother saw something she wanted in a shop window, a new teapot, a shawl, a radio, she did not buy it that day. She went home and wrote it in her kakebo. Kakebo, it means the household money book.

It is a little notebook where every yen that comes in and every yen that goes out is written down by hand, every night. Japanese housewives have kept them for more than a hundred years. If she still wanted the thing after three days, and it fit in the book, she went back and bought it. Most of the time she did not want it anymore. She said, the shop will still be there, the money might not. I keep a kakebo too, a plain notebook from the drugstore. Every night after supper, I write what I spent that day. It takes three minutes. At the end of the month, I look at it with a cup of tea, and every month I find something I do not need to pay for anymore. Writing it by hand is the trick. When you write it, you feel it. When you tap a card, you feel nothing. On the first page of every month, she wrote four questions, the same four that every kakebo asks. How much money do I have?

How much do I want to save? How much am I spending? And how can I do better? She answered them in pencil, in two or three words each. That was her whole money plan for 60 years. Number three, she stopped sitting still in the morning. At 6.30 every morning, the radio in the park played the same music and everyone in the neighborhood came out to do Rajiho Taiso. Rajiho Taiso, it means radio exercises. It is a few minutes of simple stretching and arm swinging to music, and Japan has done it on the radio since 1928. Children, mothers, old men in their undershirts, everyone. My mother went every morning until she was 96. She stood in the second row, always the same place, next to the lady from the tofu shop. In summer, the children got a stamp on a little card for every morning they came. and at the end of August, a pencil or a notebook as a prize.

We children stopped going when school started again. My mother never stopped. When she could not go to the park anymore, she did it in her kitchen, holding the edge of the table. I do it here too, every morning, in my living room, with the music on my grandson's tablet. It is gentle, nothing fancy, and you can do most of it holding a chair. Ten minutes in the morning, and the whole day starts moving. Number four, she stopped trying to win. My mother said, 負けるが勝ち It means, To lose is to win. When my brother argued with her about politics, or my sister told her she was doing the laundry wrong, she just smiled and said, Maybe you are right. Then she went on doing the laundry her way. She told me once, When you are sixty, you have already won enough arguments. Now you can let the young ones be right. It costs nothing, and the house stays quiet.

and she noticed something. When she stopped fighting, people started asking for her opinion. My brother, the same one who argued about politics, came to her 20 years later to ask what he should do about his own son. I have practiced this one for years, and it is the hardest one on the list. When my son tells me how to use my telephone, I say, Maybe you are right. When my neighbor tells me my roses need more sun, I say, Maybe you are right. Then I go inside and make tea, and I feel lighter than if I had won. Number 5. She stopped going to sleep with worries. Next to her pillow, she kept a small notebook and a pencil. Every night, before she turned off the light, she wrote down whatever was worrying her. The rent, my brother's job, the roof, a letter she had not answered. Then she closed the notebook and said out loud, Tomorrow.

The worries were on the paper now, not in her head, and the paper could wait until morning. She kept that notebook by her pillow for almost 40 years. When we cleaned out her house, we found a whole box of them. I read some on the airplane home. Most of the worries I did not even remember. The roof was fixed in 1978. My brother found a job. The letter got answered. 40 years of worries, and almost all of them came out fine. I tried it the first winter after my husband passed, when I could not sleep. Now I cannot sleep without it. Most nights I write two or three lines. In the morning, half of them look small. The other half I can do something about, with coffee and daylight. Nothing gets fixed at two in the morning. If you have a mother or a grandmother who did any of these things, please press the little thumb under this video.

and send it to someone who is turning 60 this year. It will help them more than a birthday card. Number six, she stopped saying, I am too old. At 70, my mother started Shodo, Japanese calligraphy, with a brush and black ink at the community center. At 80, she started writing haiku, little poems of 17 sounds, and she sent one to me in every letter. At 90, she learned to make origami cranes for the children at the temple school. She was never very good at any of them. That was not the point. We have a word for it, ikigai. It means, the reason you get up in the morning. She said, if you have nothing to learn, you have nothing to wake up for. I am 79, and last year I started learning to play the ukulele. My grandson laughs at me and my fingers hurt and I play very badly. But every morning, I want to get up and try again. That is ikigai.

One of the haiku my mother sent me, I still have on my refrigerator. She wrote it in Japanese, and I put it in English for you. Old Woman's Teacup Steam rises in winter light. The cat wants my lap. That is all. Nothing happens in it. She was 91 when she wrote it, and she was still looking at the steam. Number 7 She stopped staying home alone all day. Every morning after Rajio Taiso, my mother walked to the market, even if she only needed one onion. She said good morning to the fish man, the tofu lady, the boy at the rice shop. She had one rule, one real conversation every day with someone who is not family. In the afternoon she sat on the bench outside her house and the neighbors stopped to talk. When she was 99, the mailman still stopped his bicycle to ask her about her haiku.

And when a neighbor did not come out to her bench for two days, my mother went and knocked on her door. The whole street did that for each other. Nobody had to be told. Here it is harder, because everybody drives. So I go to the same little grocery store at the same time every Tuesday and Friday, and I know the cashiers by name. I volunteer at the library on Wednesdays, and I call one friend every day, even for five minutes, A day without one conversation is a day too long. Number eight, she stopped doing everything alone. When she was younger, my mother never asked anybody for anything. After 70, she changed. A high school girl from next door started carrying her rice home from the market. In return, my mother taught the girl calligraphy every Sunday. We have a word for this too, otagaisama. It means we are all in this together. You help me, I help you, and nobody owes anybody.

My mother said, letting someone help you is also a gift to them. It makes them feel needed and everybody wants to be needed at any age. So she learned to say one sentence without being ashamed. Would you help me with this please? Then she always found something to give back. I learned this one late. For years after my husband passed, I climbed the ladder to change the light bulbs myself. Then a young couple moved in next door. Now the husband does my light bulbs, and I watch their little girl after school on Thursdays. Otagai-sama, nobody is keeping score. Number nine is the one sitting in your cupboard. My mother had a set of good teacups, thin white porcelain with blue flowers, a wedding present from 1939. For 40 years they stayed in their box, wrapped in paper, waiting for a special day.

After my father died, she took them out, unwrapped them, and started using them every single morning. She said, It means, every day is a good day. I am not saving anything for later anymore. Later is not a day on the calendar. My mother drank her tea from those cups for 40 more years. Two of them broke. She did not cry. She said, they had a good life, so go to your cupboard tonight. The good cups, the good plates, the nice tablecloth, the perfume you are saving, use them tomorrow morning for nobody but you. Now, a few things that can go wrong, and it is not your fault. If you try to stop all nine at once, you will stop none. My mother took years, one at a time. Pick one this week. If you start the money book and you miss a few nights, do not throw it away. Write what you remember and keep going.

If the morning exercises feel hard, do them sitting in a chair. And if you feel lonely when you go out the first time, go to the same place at the same time every week. After a month, they will know your name and they will miss you when you do not come. If you watched my last video about staying warm in winter without turning on the heat, you already know my mother's first rule. Warm the person, not the house. All of these nine things come from the same kind of thinking. Make your life smaller and lighter so you can carry it a long way. The last time I saw my mother was her hundredth birthday. I flew to Osaka. My brothers and sisters, the grandchildren, the great-grandchildren, everybody was squeezed into her little house. In the morning, before everybody woke up, she made tea for the two of us, in the good cups, the white ones with the blue flowers.

We sat at the load table by the window. She did not say anything for a long time. Then she said, Sachiko, I have stopped worrying about you. And I said, Okasan, I have stopped worrying about you too. She laughed so hard, she spilled her tea. That was the last morning we had alone. So, the nine things my mother stopped doing after 60. 1. She stopped rushing. 2. She stopped buying on the first day and wrote everything in her money book. 3. She stopped sitting still in the morning. 4. She stopped trying to win. 5. She stopped going to sleep with worries. 6. She stopped saying, I am too old. 7. She stopped staying home alone. 8. She stopped doing everything by herself. 9. She stopped saving the good cups for later. Now tell me in the comments, which one of these nine will you stop first, starting this week?

And how old was the oldest person in your family? I read every one with my tea in my good cup. Next time, I will show you the old Japanese way of walking my mother taught me. 10 minutes a day. And why at 79 I have never needed a cane. Tomorrow morning, use the good cup. Every day is a good day. I'll see you next time.
